turns.q:
Your response was: "Looked at it. Price section didn't work. Too many numbers at too many sizes. Couldn't spot the total without reading every label."

We want to understand what you meant by "couldn't spot the total without reading every label", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The largest price on the right, "$39.99", looked more prominent than the final "$288.99" total amount below it.
B) The "Total" label was large on the left, but the matching total amount on the right did not stand out in the same way.
C) The subtotal, shipping, item prices, and total were all grouped close together, making the final total hard to distinguish at a glance.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
What specifically about the order summary layout makes the final $288.99 total blend in with the subtotal, shipping, and item prices?
turns.a: Subtotal, tax, total — all different sizes. No obvious main number. Couldn't tell which was the total at a glance.

turns.q: If the final total doesn’t stand out from the subtotal, shipping, and item prices, what would that make someone do before they feel confident about the amount being charged?
turns.a: Nearly moved on without confirming the total. Too many sizes at similar weights — couldn't tell which was the main one. Stopped and read each label to confirm.

turns.q: In this static layout, would that label-by-label checking make the order summary harder to understand only the first time, or would it keep slowing someone down every time they reviewed the amount?
turns.a: Standard checkout pattern: total as the dominant number — 18–20px, bold, clearly largest. All line items at 13–14px, same size, reads as a group not competition. Labels and footnotes at ≤11px — clearly subordinate. Three levels. Ensures scan works before read. Right now the sizes are competing instead of stepping. One CSS pass, four or five type declarations, done.
